newsitem.title: USA: Hartford searches soul in wake of Whalers' exit.
newsitem.headline: Hartford searches soul in wake of Whalers' exit.

text.p: A day after Connecticut lost its only major league sports franchise, Hartford civic leaders set about ways of keeping the capital city in the economic development ballgame.

Hartford Whalers owner Peter Karmanos on Wednesday rejected Connecticut Gov. John Rowland's proposal to build a $147 million arena, and said the National Hockey League (NHL) team would leave the state at the end of this season.
Mike Peters, Hartford's feisty ex-fireman mayor and loyal Whalers fan, said Thursday he felt the loss personally.
"I'd like to slap him in the back of the head," Peters said of Karmanos.
Peters told Reuters the Whalers' exit was a major setback for the city, both economically and for civic morale.
"It really hurts," Peters said. "It's like I've been jilted by a young lady I really loved."
The scrappy city of 126,000 has been trying to bounce back from corporate downsizing and a slew of urban woes since the late 1980s.

The Whalers contributed about a third of the $200 million a year pumped into Hartford's economy by the arts, entertainment and sports, said Anthony Caruso, executive director of the Hartford Downtown Council.
Of the 3.5 million people who attend downtown arts, entertainment and sports activities each year, about 16 percent came for the Whalers, Caruso said.
The hockey team came to Hartford in 1975 and joined the NHL four years later.

Hartford's only other experience with a major league sports team dates back to 1871-1875, when the Hartford Dark Blues played in baseball's old National Association. A day after the Whalers' exit, the local consensus was that Karmanos had already decided to move the team, in spite of what was viewed as a very generous offer by the governor.
"We're all feeling a little bit used, especially those people who've been working their butts off (to retain the Whalers)" Caruso said.

Karmanos has not said where the team, which came to Hartford in 1975, will relocate. Among the possible new homes being mentioned are Minneapolis/St. Paul; Columbus, Ohio; Nashville, and Oklahoma City.

Peters said the move was inevitable. "In this day and age, with all the sports teams moving around just for the extra buck, inevitably it's going to happen to us. It just happened a lot sooner than I thought. The state is very concerned (about downtown Hartford), so I think the resources will be there for whatever we decide on."

"The kinds of activities that will 'replace' the Whalers are already in the works," Caruso said. He said the Hartford Civic Center may be retrofitted, possibly as a conference center or much-needed banquet facility.
Caruso said metropolitan Hartford, with a population of 700,000, would make an excellent venue for another pro sports team. The city is already holding talks with minor league hockey teams.

Caruso said Hartford's Riverfront Recapture project, which has raised some $35 million in public and private money to restore the Connecticut River as an important economic and recreational resource, is nearing completion.

Peters said the Greater Hartford Arts Council is pushing to revive the downtown. "We've already defined an arts and entertainment district. We've been working very hard on creating an atmosphere where you can go down and listen to some blues, see a good show, and we'll just step that up."
Peters said Hartford had overcome obstacles in the past and would keep doing so.

"Let me tell you, we've been around for 358 years, and we're still doing pretty good. Our housing stock is getting better, the streets are cleaner, crime is down, businesses are coming in. I think we're a big-league city. We just got caught with an owner that wanted to move."
--Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224
